s1.explanation: The unit responds to a whole small-to-medium animal (dogs, foxes, monkeys) seen at a middle distance, centred and facing the camera with an alert, open-eyed face. Typical high cases are a fox or dog standing, sitting or running toward the viewer with its full body in frame. It is weak when the face fills the frame (head close-ups of kuvasz, German shepherd or Appenzeller). It is also weak when the animal is small or distant in the scene, turned away, or curled up asleep. Similar units prefer the head close-ups that this unit ignores.

s2.explanation: Responds to a whole small-to-medium canid-like animal (dog, fox) seen at medium distance, with the full body or most of it in frame and the face turned toward the camera with eyes open. It is strongest when the animal is a compact, centered figure with its face clearly visible (Arctic fox, Maltese, corgis, running terriers). It is weak for tight head close-ups (Appenzeller, kuvasz and German shepherd portraits), for tiny or distant animals, and for animals turned away or curled up asleep. Similar units prefer the head close-ups that this unit ignores.

s3.explanation: Responds to a whole, alert dog or fox (or a similar fluffy mammal) seen at a medium distance. The animal fills a good part of the frame, its full body and legs are visible, and its face looks toward the camera. Activity is high for corgis, foxes and terriers standing, running or sitting while facing the viewer. It is weak for tight head close-ups, which the similar units prefer (kuvasz, German shepherd and Appenzeller face shots). It is also weak for tiny, distant or side-on animals and for animals curled up asleep.

real_s1.explanation: The unit responds to a whole, alert, open-eyed small-to-medium animal (dogs, foxes, monkeys) shown at medium size in the frame rather than as a head close-up, and responds weakly to close-ups and to sleeping or curled-up animals.

real_s2.explanation: Responds to a whole small-to-medium dog or fox seen at medium distance, with the body mostly in frame and the face turned toward the camera with eyes open; it is weak for head-only close-ups, distant animals, and animals turned away or asleep.

real_s3.explanation: The unit responds to an alert dog or fox (or similar fluffy mammal) that faces the camera with its eyes open, standing, running or sitting upright, and not curled up asleep. Whether the whole body is shown and fairly large in the frame matters somewhat, but less than gaze and alertness.

null_s1.explanation: The unit is most active on photos of small-to-medium mammals such as dogs, foxes and monkeys. Within those classes, none of the proposed factors explains its activity: framing, whole-body visibility and alert versus sleeping posture all fail.

null_s2.explanation: The unit likely responds to small-to-medium dogs and foxes, which are the classes it is most active on, but no within-class feature tested here explains its activity. Framing, face orientation, posture and mouth state do not distinguish its stronger responses from its weaker ones.

null_s3.explanation: The unit is most active on photos of dog and fox classes (corgis, foxes, terriers and similar fluffy mammals), but within those classes none of the proposed framing or pose features (whole body, visible legs, facing the camera, upright posture) explains its activity.
